turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, Mr Meyer. Sorry about the wait, it's been one of those mornings.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Forty minutes. And the parking by the robot was a mess. I only came for the work form and this knee, I'm not in the mood for a long story.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame. Tell me about the knee first, in your own words, and we'll get to the form.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Left knee. It's a niggle, honestly, not an emergency. My manager's been on my case about the form, which doesn't help.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the soreness been there?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. No, ignore that, the left knee's been a mild niggle for six weeks, sore when I've been walking the aisles. I can't give you the actual date.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you twist it, or fall?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I just do the floor at the hardware shop, on my feet the whole shift, up and down ladders.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling, locking, or giving way?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. It doesn't lock and it hasn't given way. Just an ache by the time we knock off.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What makes it ease off?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Getting off it. If I sit for a bit, it settles. Mornings are alright.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been getting headaches with this?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't get headaches.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about chest pain, shortness of breath, or feeling dizzy?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Can we not do the whole checklist, I'm gatvol and I've still got to fetch my grandchild.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll keep it short, promise. What have you taken for the knee?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Brufen. I nearly said the two hundred milligram ones, but they're the six hundreds, one tablet when it's bad, not every day. My sister's the tablet person. She takes biotin for her hair, keeps trying to give me some, I don't touch it. And her perindopril is for her blood pressure, her bottle, not mine.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, biotin and perindopril stay hers. So just ibuprofen six hundred milligrams, as you need it, for the knee. Any diabetes, known blood pressure, operations?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes. Never been told I have high blood pressure. No operations. My dad had a stroke, if that's what you're fishing for. He was sixty-six. My sister hasn't let it go since.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry about your dad. Anyone else in the family, or just him?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Just my father. Can we carry on.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Quit smoking three years ago. Two beers on a Saturday if the rugby's on. Otherwise I can't be bothered.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Before I came in, the sister checked your blood pressure. She wrote one seventy-two over ninety-eight. That's high, so I'm going to repeat it while you're sitting.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): It's white coat. It always shoots up in here. At the chemist it's fine. I'm not ill.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, this cuff reads one fifty-eight over ninety-four. Pulse is seventy-six, regular. Better than the sister's number, still on the high side.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): See, it drops when you lot stop fussing. I'm not starting tablets over that.

[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I agree we're not starting blood pressure tablets today. Two clinic readings, and you reckoning it's white coat, isn't a diagnosis. What we need is a run of readings away from the rooms.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't own a machine. I'm not buying a fancy one this month either, money's tight.

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): You don't have to buy one today. Use the machine at Clicks or Dis-Chem, or borrow your sister's cuff, not her pills. Morning and evening, sit quietly five minutes, write the figures down, and bring them in two weeks.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Homework. Ja, fine. Two weeks.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has anyone looked at cholesterol or sugar recently?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometime last year, don't ask me the month, could've been March, I really don't know. Finger prick at Dis-Chem. Chap said the cholesterol was six point two, no, five point eight. Borderline. No tablets from them.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So a pharmacy finger-prick, called borderline at five point eight, not something I can treat off. If those home readings stay high we might send a proper fasting cholesterol. Not today.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. I don't want extra needles on top of this form nonsense.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's look at the left knee. No swelling, and the skin isn't red. You're tender on the inner joint line. Bend and straighten are full, and it feels stable when I push on it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, that inner spot is the one. Rest of it doesn't bother me.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Earlier you said the headaches weren't a thing. Has that stayed true this past week?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, no. Most afternoons this past week my head's been thumping, a dull ache across the forehead. I blamed the heat and being tired, which is why I said no. But it's been happening.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks for correcting that. Any nausea with it, or a change in your eyesight?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No nausea. Eyes are fine. It fades once I'm home and sitting down.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. To my mind the left knee is a straightforward overload on the inner side, nothing today that needs a scan. The blood pressure is up here, and white coat is possible, but I'm not diagnosing hypertension off these two readings.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So the form. Work wants it to say I can stay on the floor. If you block it my manager's going to have a fit.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll complete the knee part. You can keep working, ice it after the shift, and take that ibuprofen with food. I won't put down that your blood pressure is normal. Come back in a month with the diary, actually no, come in two weeks, I'd rather see the numbers sooner.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks it is. If the knee's quiet by then, do I still come all this way?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still come, mainly for the pressure diary. If you get chest pain, a headache that hits like a thunderclap, or the knee suddenly swells and you can't walk, skip the appointment and go to casualty.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I hear you. The thunderclap thing, not the ordinary afternoon one.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Exactly, the ordinary afternoon ache we already know about. The form will be at reception when you leave. I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Reception. Fine. I need to get on, the grandchild's waiting and the traffic's going to be horrible.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
